On April 15, 1872, the charter for the city was filed. Deed records show that many of Colonel Savoy's town lots were sold for $150, $200, and some for $250. He donated the lot upon which the Methodist Episcopal Church was built.

Before moving to Fannin County, Colonel Savoy had been twice married. His second wife came with him to his new home where he reared a family of seven.¹⁰

In 1880 Colonel Savoy's health failed and he went to a health resort, but died on the way at the town of Johnson City and was buried there in August. Mrs. Savoy survived him two decades. His grave is dated August 7, 1908.¹¹

THE SAVOY OF THE COLLEGE PERIOD.—The richness of the surrounding territory and the advent of the railroad made the new town to grow fast. The old town, which was completely destroyed by a cyclone in 1850, it was quickly rebuilt; by 1882 it had become a lively and prosperous town.

Probably the next largest town to Honey Grove, in point of size and commerce, in Savoy. This town has built up very rapidly since the Texas and Pacific Railroad, on which it is situated, about four miles west of Sherman at a town called Bells in Grayson County, running a southeast direction. It is a chartered institution, and perhaps takes the lead of all colleges in the county. The churches and institutions of worship in the matter of church buildings are meager. One hundred still standing, the different denominations.¹²

Mrs. Savoy, the second wife, born Tallulah Clark, was a soldier in the Spanish-American War and died in San Francisco. He had a daughter who was born and raised in Mexico.
